content: Following the administration of 30 mg of levocetirizine once daily for six days in nine elderly subjects aged 65 to 74 years, the total body clearance of the drug was approximately 33% lower compared to younger adults. The pharmacokinetics of racemic cetirizine have been shown to depend on renal function rather than age, and this finding is also applicable to levocetirizine, as both drugs are predominantly excreted unchanged in the urine. Therefore, the dosage of levocetirizine dihydrochloride should be adjusted in elderly patients based on their renal function. Pharmacokinetic data from 77 patients (40 men and 37 women) were analyzed to assess the potential effect of gender. The half-life of levocetirizine was slightly shorter in women (7.08 ± 1.72 hours) compared to men (8.62 ± 1.84 hours). However, the body weight-adjusted oral clearance was comparable between women (0.67 ± 0.16 mL/min/kg) and men (0.59 ± 0.12 mL/min/kg). The same daily doses and dosing intervals are applicable for men and women with normal renal function. The effect of race on levocetirizine pharmacokinetics has not been studied. Since levocetirizine is primarily excreted renally and there are no significant racial differences in creatinine clearance, its pharmacokinetic characteristics are not expected to differ across races. No race-related differences in the kinetics of racemic cetirizine have been observed.8-fold, 3.2-fold, 4.3-fold, and 5.7-fold in mild, moderate, severe, and end-stage renal disease (ESRD) patients, respectively, compared to healthy subjects. Corresponding increases in half-life were 1.4-fold, 2.0-fold, 2.9-fold, and 4-fold, respectively. Total body clearance of levocetirizine after oral dosing was correlated with creatinine clearance and progressively reduced with increasing severity of renal impairment. Therefore, dose and dosing intervals should be adjusted based on creatinine clearance in patients with mild, moderate, or severe renal impairment. Levocetirizine is contraindicated in patients with ESRD (CLCR < 10 mL/min). During a standard 4-hour hemodialysis session, less than 10% of levocetirizine is removed. Dosage should be reduced in patients with mild renal impairment, and both dosage and frequency of administration should be reduced in those with moderate or severe renal impairment. Levocetirizine dihydrochloride has not been studied in patients with hepatic impairment. Non-renal clearance, indicative of hepatic contribution, accounts for approximately 28% of total body clearance in healthy adults after oral administration. Since levocetirizine is mainly excreted unchanged by the kidneys, its clearance is unlikely to be significantly reduced in patients with solely hepatic impairment. No carcinogenicity studies have been conducted with levocetirizine. However, cetirizine carcinogenicity studies are relevant for assessing the carcinogenic potential of levocetirizine. In a 2-year carcinogenicity study in rats, cetirizine was not carcinogenic at dietary doses up to 20 mg/kg (approximately 15 times the maximum recommended daily oral dose in adults, 10 times in children aged 6 to 11 years, and 15 times in children aged 6 months to 5 years on a mg/m² basis). In a 2-year carcinogenicity study in mice, cetirizine caused an increased incidence of benign hepatic tumors in males at a dietary dose of 16 mg/kg (approximately 6 times the maximum recommended daily oral dose in adults, 4 times in children aged 6 to 11 years, and 6 times in children aged 6 months to 5 years on a mg/m² basis). No increased incidence of benign tumors was observed at a dietary dose of 4 mg/kg (approximately 2 times the maximum recommended daily oral dose in adults, equivalent to the maximum recommended daily oral dose in children aged 6 to 11 years, and 2 times in children aged 6 months to 5 years on a mg/m² basis). The clinical significance of these findings during long-term use of levocetirizine dihydrochloride is unknown. Levocetirizine was not mutagenic in the Ames test and not clastogenic in the human lymphocyte assay, the mouse lymphoma assay, or the in vivo micronucleus test in mice. In a fertility and general reproductive performance study in mice, cetirizine did not impair fertility at an oral dose of 64 mg/kg (approximately 25 times the recommended daily oral dose in adults on a mg/m² basis). In reproductive toxicology studies, levocetirizine was not teratogenic in rats and rabbits at oral doses up to 200 mg/kg and 120 mg/kg, respectively (approximately 320 and 390 times the maximum recommended daily oral dose in adults on a mg/m² basis). In mice, cetirizine caused retarded pup weight gain during lactation at an oral dose in dams of 96 mg/kg (approximately 40 times the maximum recommended daily oral dose in adults on a mg/m² basis). The efficacy of levocetirizine dihydrochloride for treating uncomplicated skin manifestations of chronic idiopathic urticaria was evaluated in two multicenter, randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind clinical trials of 4 weeks' duration in adult patients aged 18 to 85 years. These trials included one 4-week dose-ranging trial and one 4-week single-dose level efficacy trial, involving 423 patients (139 males and 284 females). Most patients (>90%) were Caucasian, with a mean age of 41 years. Of these patients, 146 received levocetirizine dihydrochloride 5 mg once daily in the evening. Efficacy was assessed based on patient-recorded pruritus severity on a scale of 0 to 3 (0 = none, 3 = severe). The primary efficacy endpoint was the mean reflective pruritus severity score over the first week and the entire treatment period. Additional efficacy variables included instantaneous pruritus severity score, number and size of wheals, and duration of pruritus. In the dose-ranging trial, levocetirizine dihydrochloride at doses of 2.5 mg, 5 mg, and 10 mg once daily demonstrated a greater decrease in reflective pruritus severity score compared to placebo, with statistically significant differences for all three doses. In the single-dose level trial, levocetirizine dihydrochloride 5 mg once daily showed a greater decrease from baseline in reflective pruritus severity score compared to placebo, with a statistically significant difference. Duration of pruritus, number and size of wheals, and instantaneous pruritus severity score also showed significant improvement over placebo. The significant improvement in instantaneous pruritus severity score over placebo confirmed end-of-dosing interval efficacy. No clinical efficacy trials have been conducted in pediatric patients with chronic idiopathic urticaria.
